summary: A first-person narrator shares a dinner with a woman who offers him a bite of very spicy food, which he takes and finds overwhelming. She explains the Scoville heat scale, comparing the dish to Tabasco, pepper spray and Scotch Bonnet peppers, and says extreme heat releases endorphins. The two then walk toward Dolores Park, where the narrator notes a buzzing crowd and the growing attraction between them. The excerpt is part 105 of a longer work titled Book 1.
one_line: A narrator tries an extremely spicy dish with a woman, learns about the Scoville scale, and walks with her toward a crowded Dolores Park.
key_facts: The narrator says he likes spicy food and always orders curries with four chilies at Pakistani restaurants.
He took a big bite of the woman's food and called it a big mistake.
The woman handed the narrator her horchata, which he used to ease the burning.
The woman explains that pure capsaicin measures about 15 million Scovilles.
Tabasco is said to be about 50,000 Scovilles on the Scoville scale.
Pepper spray is described as a healthy three million Scovilles.
The dish is described as a puny 200,000 Scovilles, about as hot as a mild Scotch Bonnet Pepper.
The woman says she worked up to this level of heat in about a year.
She claims extreme peppers near one million Scovilles make the brain awash in endorphins, a better body-stone than hash.
The woman jokes that the narrator is insane and that his hobby is building and smashing laptops.
The woman offers the narrator her mister, and he declines with the word Pass.
When they walk toward Dolores Park, the narrator notices he is now tall enough that his arm fits around her shoulders.
The narrator says the girls he dated were all his height because teenaged girls grow faster than guys.
Near the park, the two feel a buzz like the hum of a million bees from the crowd streaming toward it.
The walk toward Dolores Park begins after turning the corner on 20th Street.
